2.1. Comparative hardship is a relevant factor for de- A
termining the question as to·whether the requirement of
the landlord is bona fide or not within the meaning of tha
provisions of the said Act and the Rules. It is essentially
a question of fact. Such a question of fact, however, is to
be determined on the touchstone of the statutory provi- B
sions as contained in s.21 (1 )(a) and Rules 16(2)(c) of the
Rules. [Para 13] [549-C,D]
2.2. Rule 1 q provides for some factors which are re-quired to be taken into consideration for the purpose of
determining the comparative hardship. Respondent No. C
3 in this case does not have any business. If he has no
business, the question of application of the factors as
envisaged in the first part of clause (c) of Sub-Rule (2) of
Rule 16 will not arise. On the findings of the Appellate
Authority, no accommodation is available with him. The D
question of thus any premises beirig let out in favour of
1st appellant also does riot arise. [Para 14] [549-D,E,F]

the last so many years the appellant had made any effort
to find out a tenanted premises for herself so that she can E
continue with her business. No such material at least has
been brought on record. Any subsequent event as re-gards thereto has neither been pleaded nor proved. [Para
15] [549-F,G]
2.4. The provisions of the statutory rules must be
interpreted so as to give effect to the object and purport
of the Act. It cannot be applied in a vacuum, as the stat-F
ute requires comparison of the hardship of both the ten-ant as also the landlord. It is, therefore, not a case where G
Rule 16 has any application. [Para 15] [549-G,H, 550-A]
2.5. The Court would not determine a question only
on the basis of sympathy or sentiment. Stricto sensu eq-uity as such may not have any role to play. [Para 16] [550-

. ,, 8. Section 21 (1 )(a) of the Act reads as under:-
"21. Proceedings for release of building under
occupation oftenant.-(1) The prescribed authority may,
on an application of the landlord in that behalf, order the c
eviction of a tenant from the building under tenancy or any
specified part thereof if it is satisfied that any of the
following grounds exists namely-
(a) that the building is bona fide required either in its existing D
• -;, form or after demolition and new construction by the
landlord for occupation by himself or any member of his
family, or any person for whose benefit it is held by him,
either for residential purposes or for purposes of any
profession, trade or calling, or where the landlord is the
E trustee of a public charitable trust, for the objects of the
trust;"
The fourth proviso appended thereto reads as under:
-'- "Provided also that the prescribed authority shall, except
F • in cases provided for in the Explanation, take into account
the likely hardship to the tenant from the grant of the
application as against the likely hardship to the landlord
from the refusal of the application and for that purpose
shall have regard to such factors as may be prescribed."
Section 41 of the Act 13 of 1972 provides for the rule mak-G
r ing power. Pursuant thereto or in furtherance thereof Rules have
been framed by the State of U.P. known as U.P. Urban Build-ings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 (for

9. Application of the aforementioned provisions to the fact B

E before us that the aforementioned finding of the Appellant Au-thority must be held to be containing an error of record, and

We may now consider the submission of Mr. Gupta,

for determining the question as to whether the requirement of
the landlord is bona fide or not within the meaning of the provi-sions of the said Act and the Rules. It is essentially a question ... of fact. Such a question of fact, however, is to be determined D
on the touchstone of the statutory pmvisions as contained in
Section 21(1)(a) and Rules 16(2)(c) of the Rules.
14. Rule 16 provides for some factors which are required
to be taken into consideration for the purpose of determining E the comparative hardship. Respondent No. 3 in this case does
not have any business. If he has no business, the question of
application of the factors as envisaged in the first part of clause
(c) of Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 16 will not arise. On the findings of .... the Appellate Authority, no accommodation is available with him . •
The question of thus any premises being let out in favour of 1 •

The provisions of the statutory rules must be interpreted

(2) SCC 300], this Court distinguishing the earlier decision of

"It was also pointed out in this case that the provisions of

their education were unemployed and wanted to carry on
business for self-employment. Secondly, as already seen
above, it was not a case where the provisions of Rule
16(2) can be said to have been ignored by the District

attempt to seek an alternative accommodation and was
unablE;! to get it."
The 'thirdly' referred to therein applies to the fact of this

Yet again in Rishi Kumar _Govil vs. Maqsoodan & ors.

"11. In the/ case in hand we find that even though the

account in context with other facts and circumstances of
the case. It cannot be a sole criterion or deciding factor
... ... to order or not the eviction of the tenant. Considering the D facts in the light of Rule 16 pressed into service on behalf
of the respondent, we find that according to the guidelines
provided therein balance tilts in favour of the unemployed
son of the landlady whose need is certainly bona fide and
has also been so accepted by the respondent before us."
E

by LRs. Vs. Union of India (UOI) and Anr. reported in 2008 (6)

"It is trite to say that legislation which may be quite
reasonable and rationale at the time of its enactment may
with the lapse of time and/or due to change of
circumstances become arbitrary, unreasonable and G
_. t violative of the doctrine of equity and even if the validity of
such legislation may have been upheld at a giyen point of
time, the Court may, in subsequent litigation, strike down
